cards.a: Nodes are interconnected with direct links — either full mesh (every node connected to every other) or partial mesh (only some pairs). Mesh gives the most redundancy and best path diversity, at the cost of many links.

cards.q: How many links does a full mesh of N nodes need, and when is each form used?
cards.a: Full mesh needs N(N-1)/2 links and is used for small cores or key hub HA, since cost dominates beyond about 5-6 nodes. Partial mesh uses a subset (hub-and-spoke with extras) for WAN cores, ISP backbones, and data centers.

cards.q: Why does mesh topology exist? What benefits does it provide?
cards.a: It provides path redundancy (a link failure is handled by another path), no single point of failure for a meshed node, lower hop count/lower latency from near-complete connectivity, and load-balancing possibilities via equal-cost multipath.

cards.q: What mechanisms make L2 mesh safe, and why?
cards.a: At L2, redundancy creates loops, so Spanning Tree (STP) puts redundant links in Blocking to prevent broadcast storms, and EtherChannel bundles two links into one logical link.

cards.q: How do L3 routing protocols realize the benefit of mesh?
cards.a: Routing protocols such as OSPF/BGP learn multiple equal paths and use ECMP (equal-cost multipath) to balance across parallel links, enabling fast convergence when a path disappears.

cards.q: Name the real-world examples where mesh is deployed.
cards.a: WAN partial mesh (backup circuits between major sites), ISP backbone (national meshes enabling sub-50 ms convergence on a fiber cut), data-center spine-leaf (full-mesh underlay between spines/leaves), and wireless mesh (APs relaying to each other to extend coverage).

cards.q: What commands implement ECMP for two equal-cost default routes?
cards.a: Configure both routes with the same AD/metric: 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.1' and 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.2'. 'show ip route' lists both, and CEF load-balances across them.

cards.q: How do you bundle two links between the same pair of switches instead of leaving STP to block one?
cards.a: Use EtherChannel: create a Port-channel interface and add both physical ports with 'channel-group 1 mode active' (LACP) on each member.

cards.q: Calculate the full-mesh link count for 4 nodes. What is the formula?
cards.a: The formula is N(N-1)/2, so 4 nodes gives 4(3)/2 = 6 links.

cards.q: What happens if you create L2 mesh redundancy without STP or EtherChannel?
cards.a: The redundancy creates loops that can cause broadcast storms. The design must control redundancy with STP or EtherChannel.

cards.q: Is full mesh the default for small networks?
cards.a: No. Full mesh for 20 routers is absurd; partial mesh or hub-spoke is typical for small networks. Full mesh is reserved for small cores/key hubs.

cards.q: What condition must hold for ECMP to balance across two routes?
cards.a: The routes must have equal AD (administrative distance) and equal metric, so both are considered equal-cost paths.

cards.q: What is a known trade-off of wireless mesh relaying?
cards.a: Wireless mesh relays degrade with hops — some technologies halve throughput per hop — so multihop relay is a trap in RF questions.

cards.q: In the mesh Quick Review, how do full mesh and partial mesh compare?
cards.a: Full mesh uses N(N-1)/2 links with redundancy for every pair but cost grows fast; it suits small cores/spines and makes ECMP easy. Partial mesh uses a selected subset with moderate cost and is typical for WAN/ISP backbones. Both need STP/EtherChannel at L2 to control loops.
